lines.text: Daily life is built from hundreds of small actions, and advanced English speakers distinguish between them with remarkable precision. Morning routines alone involve a cascade of specific verbs: you yawn, stretch, stumble out of bed, shuffle to the bathroom, splash water on your face, brush your teeth, comb or style your hair, and get dressed. Cooking demands its own vocabulary: you chop vegetables, dice onions, slice bread, grate cheese, stir soup, whisk eggs, simmer sauces, and roast meat. Household chores introduce further specificity: you sweep the floor, mop the tiles, vacuum the carpet, dust the shelves, scrub the bathtub, hang out the washing, fold the laundry, and iron the shirts. Even sitting has variations — you perch on the edge of a chair, slouch on a sofa, recline in an armchair, or squat to reach a low shelf. Eating verbs distinguish manner: you nibble a biscuit (eat in small bites), gobble your lunch (eat greedily and fast), sip tea (drink slowly), gulp water (drink quickly in large amounts), and savour a fine meal (eat slowly, appreciating the flavour). The difference between basic and advanced English often comes down to these precise daily verbs — they transform generic descriptions into vivid, natural-sounding language that native speakers use instinctively.
